readings.title: Booking a health visit by telephone
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood clinic introduced online appointments. Some older patients preferred calling, but the phone line became busy each morning. The main obstacle was too many calls during one short period. Patients believed early calls were their only chance, even when appointments were available later in the day. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a record of call times and appointment choices. Receptionists counted unanswered calls and asked callers which types of visit they needed. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated routine requests could be handled throughout the day. Urgent calls were mixed with repeat bookings, although the two required different responses. The group then introduced separate call guidance for urgent and routine needs. The clinic published clear hours and kept a telephone route for patients who did not use the internet. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: digital options should expand access. A new booking method is useful only when it does not remove a practical route for existing patients. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in booking a health visit by telephone, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Understanding a medicine label
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A pharmacy gave patients a printed schedule for regular medicine. Several customers returned because the small symbols were unclear. The main obstacle was instructions that depended on tiny icons. People could read the medicine name but were unsure whether a symbol referred to meals or times of day. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a short explanation trial with customers. Pharmacists asked volunteers to describe the label in their own words without taking any medical decisions for them. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated plain words were recalled more accurately. Patients understood a direct sentence better than a row of similar pictures. The group then introduced larger print and complete written instructions. Qualified staff checked each revised label and remained available to explain individual prescriptions. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: health communication must be tested for understanding. Attractive symbols cannot replace a clear explanation of information that people need to use safely. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in understanding a medicine label, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A video consultation at the library
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A rural district offered remote health conversations from a library room. Residents welcomed shorter journeys but worried about privacy. The main obstacle was a room where conversations could be overheard. The screen faced a shared corridor, and visitors had to explain their purpose at a public desk. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a walk-through of the appointment process. Staff followed a visitor from arrival to departure and invited comments on every step. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated the entrance procedure caused most concern. People trusted the clinician, yet disliked identifying their health visit in front of others. The group then introduced a neutral booking name and a screened doorway. The library kept the room quiet and provided a private way to ask for technical help. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: privacy includes the whole service journey. A secure video connection alone cannot protect a consultation if arrival arrangements reveal personal details. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a video consultation at the library, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Teaching a simple health app
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A voluntary group helped older residents read clinic messages on a phone. Its first class moved too quickly for new users. The main obstacle was a lesson that assumed shared starting skills. Some learners needed help with basic screen controls while others were ready to practise finding a message. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used observations from two small practice groups. Tutors noted where learners paused and asked which tasks they wanted to repeat independently. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated practice time mattered more than extra features. Participants gained confidence when they completed one useful action without being rushed. The group then introduced short sessions with optional individual support. The group prepared printed steps and allowed people to practise without entering private medical information. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: confidence grows from manageable success. A lesson becomes accessible when learners can move at a pace suited to their own experience. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in teaching a simple health app, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning digital health and older adults often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the community health information service. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关数字健康与老年服务的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the community health team proposing a small improvement to the community health information service. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community health information service. People have noticed too many calls during one short period, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
